(2006) showcased the potential of mechanistic models, specifically ASM1, for feedforward NHx control, their inherent limitations in isolation are acknowledged. A significant stride towards addressing these limitations is the development of hybrid models, which combine mechanistic and data-driven components. These models offer the potential to overcome simplifying assumptions that degrade mechanistic model performance, thereby enhancing their forecasting capabilities in real-world operational scenarios. For these reasons, due to expected superior extrapolation accuracy, and to allow building on Vrečko’s work, a hybrid model was used in this case. For nearly a decade, identical feedback ABAC and feedforward-feedback methanol dosing controllers have been employed in parallel process trains. Yet, the HRSD NTP consistently observes substantial differences in air and methanol demands between these trains. These 52 The Water Research Foundation )N-L/gm( xHN ffe TA time (7 days total) NHx observations NHx setpoint disparities suggest underlying variations between the parallel reactors, possibly due to uneven load distribution. Furthermore, inconsistencies between handheld and in-situ DO measurements question the accuracy of the latter in representing overall zone conditions. These challenges highlight the limitations of a mechanistic model that relies on assumptions of equal load distribution, which would affect parallel train-to-train model performance, and representative DO data, which would affect the whole-plant model performance. In reality, numerous factors likely contribute to mechanistic model inaccuracies, and these hypothesized issues represent only two. The other contributing factors are simply unknown.
